title: In the woods
hook: in the woods we return to reason and faith (Nature 1)

segments.voice: Yesterday, once in a thousand years: the stars come out every night, and so we stop looking. Your line was once in a thousand years. What did you see as if for the first time? Day one thousand one hundred eighty-nine.

Reason and faith. Put those two words side by side at a dinner table and you might start an argument, with someone casting them as rivals. Emerson, in the first chapter of Nature, puts them in the same sentence, on the same path, among trees. He doesn't say the woods give you one or the other. He says you get both back. And the word he uses is return, as though both were yours once, and you wandered off. Today, in the woods.
screen: `REASON AND FAITH.` → `CAST AS RIVALS.` → `IN THE SAME SENTENCE.`

segments.voice: First, the age you are in the woods. "In the woods, is perpetual youth." Emerson says that in the woods a person sheds their years the way a snake sheds its skin, and at any age is a child again. Not childish. Fresh. Second, the line itself. "In the woods, we return to reason and faith." Reason: the clear, unhurried mind that can see what's true. Faith: trust, a sense that the world holds together. Emerson doesn't make them fight. He says both come back when the noise drops away. Third, the promise. In the same passage he says that among the trees he feels nothing can happen to him in life, no disgrace, no disaster, that nature can't repair, as long as he keeps his eyes. That's a big claim, and it's his, from a man who had buried his young wife. He isn't saying nothing will hurt. He's saying the woods are a place where repair begins. Fourth, where the paragraph goes next. Standing on bare ground, he writes, all mean egotism vanishes. "I become a transparent eye-ball; I am nothing; I see all." The self gets small, and the seeing gets large. Some readers laugh at that eyeball. But the point under it is simple: among trees, you stop being the center of the picture. Far from any forest, that might be a single tree on a city street, a park at lunch, a row of bushes by a bus stop. The woods can be smaller than we think.
screen: `IN THE WOODS, IS PERPETUAL YOUTH.` · `REASON AND FAITH COME BACK.` · `NOTHING NATURE CANNOT REPAIR.` · `A TRANSPARENT EYE-BALL.` · then, large: `IN THE WOODS, WE RETURN TO REASON AND FAITH.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: walk among trees. If you can, go outside now and walk slowly toward the nearest tree, or under a few. If you can't, sit and bring to mind the last time you stood among trees: the smell, the light through leaves, the sound underfoot. Either way, let your mind get quiet enough to notice two things: something clear, and something steady. You don't have to name them reason and faith. Just notice them. The bell holds the time.
In the woods. Emerson's place of perpetual youth, where, he says, we return to reason and faith, and the self becomes a transparent eye. Today's word.
Your line: in the woods. Today, find one tree on your way somewhere, stop under it for a few breaths, and let yourself be small. Day one thousand one hundred eighty-nine.

howItsDone: Readers of Emerson's Nature often take walks among trees as a quiet practice of their own, sometimes carrying this passage with them, to let reason and trust settle at the same time.

notes: Three quotations from Nature, ch. 1; confirm wording and punctuation (including 'eye-ball' with the hyphen) against the first edition.
Writer cut a line about friends teasing Emerson over the transparent eyeball (the Cranch caricature); 'some readers laugh at that eyeball' remains and could also be cut.
'A man who had buried his young wife' refers back to day 1186.
The closing line ('the woods can be smaller than we think') replaces a general claim about Concord; fine to cut.
The hook says reason and faith are often framed as rivals ('people say'); this is a light framing of everyday talk, not a claim about any tradition; soften if needed.

Editor pass: hook softened from 'one belongs to the lab, people say, the other to the church' (a sweeping claim about what people think) to 'someone casting them as rivals'; 'on an ordinary day' (stock turn of the block) changed to 'far from any forest'.
